title: Remote Work Is Making People Lonelier — and the Effects Are Worst for Those Living Alone
excerpt: A landmark study of 588,000 workers published in Science found that remote work accounts for roughly a third of the post-pandemic rise in mental distress. For NRI tech workers far from family, the findings hit close to home.
body:
The convenience of working from home has always come with an implicit trade: flexibility for solitude. For most of the post-pandemic era, that trade was treated as an obvious win.

Now a major study published in the journal *Science* suggests the costs may be higher than anyone appreciated — and for people living alone, the toll on mental health is substantial.

## The Largest Study of Its Kind

Researchers from the Federal Reserve Bank of New York, the University of Virginia, and Harvard University analyzed five nationally representative surveys spanning 2011 to 2024, covering **588,322 American workers**. They excluded the acute pandemic years of 2020 and 2021 to isolate the structural effects of remote work from the chaos of lockdowns.

Their approach was straightforward: classify occupations as "remotable" (software engineering, law, finance) or "non-remotable" (nursing, retail, construction), then compare how workers in each category fared on measures of social isolation and psychological distress before and after the pandemic.

The differences were stark.

Workers in remotable jobs now spend roughly **one additional hour alone per workday** compared to pre-pandemic levels. They socialize less after work. And they are significantly more likely to go entire days without a single face-to-face interaction.

Among workers in remotable jobs who live alone, the likelihood of spending the entire day without social contact rose by **7 percentage points — an 83 percent increase**.

## A Third of the Mental Health Crisis

The isolation didn't stay abstract. Scores on the Kessler K-6 scale, a clinical measure of generalized psychological distress, rose by 0.1 standard deviations for workers in remotable jobs relative to those in non-remotable jobs. The increase was roughly **twice as large** for those living alone.

The study estimated that remote work accounts for approximately **one-third of the overall post-pandemic rise in mental distress** — a staggering share for a single structural change in how work is organized.

Other measures confirmed the pattern: workers in remotable jobs showed increased rates of depression, higher mental health care utilization, and more antidepressant prescriptions. Crucially, they did *not* show similar increases in non-mental-health doctor visits or prescriptions like statins, ruling out the possibility that the increase was just due to greater flexibility to see doctors.

"That amount of isolation could have pretty detrimental mental health impacts," said co-author Emma Harrington, an economist at the University of Virginia.

## Not a Case for Return-to-Office Mandates

The study's authors and independent experts have been careful to note that the findings don't justify blanket in-office mandates. Stanford economist Nicholas Bloom, whose own randomized trials found that hybrid work *improved* worker satisfaction and mental health, pointed out that the key is choice.

"The simple story is when people can work from home, they can reduce commuting stress, control their time better and have more time with friends and family," Bloom said. "The best way to improve people's mental health is: let them choose."

The *Science* study itself acknowledged the nuance: remote work offers real benefits in reduced commuting time, greater accessibility for people with disabilities, and more time with family for those who have it nearby.

But for the growing segment of workers who live alone — about 28 percent of American households — the loss of the workplace as a social anchor may be quietly hollowing out their support systems.

## The NRI Dimension

The findings carry particular resonance for the Indian diaspora, especially the large cohort of tech workers in the US on H-1B and L-1 visas.

Many are in their 20s and 30s, working in precisely the "remotable" occupations the study identifies as highest risk. A significant number live alone — far from family, with social networks constrained by visa-related job dependence and the sheer logistics of building a life in a new country.

The compound effect is a form of isolation that goes beyond what the study's US-born respondents typically experience: the everyday loneliness of remote work, layered on top of the deeper loneliness of immigration.

Previous research from the Household Pulse Survey found that people working remotely 3 or more days per week had **16 percent higher odds** of reporting higher loneliness categories, regardless of other factors. For NRI workers whose in-office days may also lack deep social connection — cultural barriers, unfamiliar social norms, the absence of family gatherings — even hybrid arrangements may not fully bridge the gap.

## What Can Be Done

The study's implicit message is that workplaces once provided something more than a paycheck: they provided social infrastructure. As a commentary in *Science* put it, remote work represents "a large-scale removal of an unpriced social good."

For those who recognize themselves in the data — working from home, living alone, realizing that days sometimes pass without meaningful human contact — the research suggests some practical steps:

Prioritize in-person social activities outside work. Choose hybrid over fully remote when possible. Seek out co-working spaces, community groups, or even regular coffee shop routines that create opportunities for face-to-face interaction.

And for the diaspora community specifically: invest in the local Indian community infrastructure — temple visits, cricket club weekends, dinner rotations with fellow immigrants — not as nostalgia, but as a genuine mental health strategy backed by data showing that isolation is more dangerous than most people realize.
